title: Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 1: Why the Way We Pay for Healthcare Is Breaking the System (And How Paying for Value Could Fix It)
summary: This is Module 1 of the HTR Academy five-part course ‘Value-Based Care Fundamentals.’ It explains, in plain language, the structural difference between fee-for-service and value-based care payment models, examines how fee-for-service created the conditions for the U.S. healthcare crisis, and builds the case — supported by comparative international data, specific program examples, and all five HTR analytical pillars — for why value-based care represents the most credible systemic reform pathway available. No prior finance or policy background is required. By the end of this module, learners will be able to explain both models to a non-clinical colleague, identify the specific incentive failure at the heart of fee-for-service, and name three federal programs actively moving the U.S. healthcare system toward value.

children.text: Imagine you hired a plumber to fix a leaky pipe, and you paid them by the hour. Now imagine that plumber was also the one who decided how long the job would take, which tools were necessary, and whether a second visit was required. You’d have a plumber with a perfectly legal, perfectly rational financial incentive to take longer, use more tools, and come back as often as possible — not because they are dishonest, but because the payment structure rewards activity, not outcomes. Your pipe gets fixed, eventually. But you pay far more than you should, and the plumber has no particular reason to make sure the fix lasts. This is, in essence, how the United States has paid for healthcare for most of the last century. The model is called fee-for-service. And understanding why it produces the results it does — the highest healthcare spending in the world paired with some of the worst outcomes among wealthy nations — is the foundation of everything we cover in this course.
The U.S. Healthcare Crisis in Numbers: Setting the Stage

Before we can understand what value-based care is trying to fix, we need to understand the scale of what is broken. The United States spent $4.5 trillion on healthcare in 2023 — approximately $13,500 per person, per year. That is nearly twice what Germany spends per capita, more than twice what the United Kingdom spends, and 30% more than Switzerland, the second most expensive healthcare system in the developed world. If the U.S. healthcare system were a country unto itself, it would be the fifth-largest economy on earth. By 2032, CMS actuaries project total U.S. healthcare spending will reach $7.2 trillion annually, consuming approximately 20 cents of every dollar the entire U.S. economy produces.

Here is where the story becomes genuinely troubling: that extraordinary level of spending does not buy extraordinary health. The United States ranks 46th in the world in life expectancy, behind not just Western European nations but also Chile, Costa Rica, and Cuba. The U.S. maternal mortality rate — the number of women who die during or shortly after childbirth — is 32.9 per 100,000 live births, compared to 4.2 in Norway, 5.0 in Sweden, and 8.8 in the United Kingdom. Among Americans who survive to age 65, health outcomes relative to peer nations are somewhat better — but this is largely attributable to universal Medicare coverage, which provides a structural floor that the under-65 population lacks. The conclusion that health economists have reached, consistently, across decades of comparative research, is that the U.S. does not have a healthcare quality problem. It has a healthcare value problem. We are spending the most and getting among the least, and the primary structural reason is how we pay.

The United States spends more on healthcare per capita than any other nation on earth — and yet ranks 64th globally in healthcare access and quality as measured by the Global Burden of Disease study. The gap between what we spend and what we get is not a clinical failure. It is a payment architecture failure. — Commonwealth Fund International Health Policy Survey, 2025.
Fee-for-Service: What It Is and Why It Made Sense Once

Fee-for-service (FFS) is a payment model in which a healthcare provider — a hospital, a physician, a laboratory, or a therapist — is paid a separate, fixed fee for each individual service they deliver. You come in for a physical exam: the doctor bills a code for the exam. The doctor orders a blood test: the lab bills a code for each component of the panel. The doctor finds something concerning and refers you to a specialist: the specialist bills for the consultation. You end up in the hospital: the hospital bills for the admission, for each day you stay, for each procedure performed, and for each medication administered. Each service generates a separate claim, each claim generates a separate payment, and the more services that are delivered, the more total revenue the provider earns. There is no mechanism within fee-for-service that rewards a doctor for keeping you healthy enough that you never needed that specialist referral in the first place.

Fee-for-service was not designed maliciously. It emerged from a logical place in the early history of American medicine, when the primary challenge was access — getting doctors and hospitals built, staffed, and financially sustainable enough to serve a growing industrial population. Paying per service was a simple, auditable, scalable mechanism that worked reasonably well in an era when healthcare was episodic: you got sick, you saw a doctor, you got better, and the transaction was complete. The model’s structural flaws only became catastrophic when the nature of disease in America fundamentally changed. By the 1980s, the leading drivers of healthcare spending were no longer acute infectious diseases or traumatic injuries — they were chronic conditions like diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, conditions that are managed over years and decades rather than treated in a single episode. Fee-for-service has no payment mechanism for management. It has only payment for treatment.
The Incentive Problem: When Doing More Pays More

The central structural failure of fee-for-service is an incentive misalignment between what is financially rewarded and what produces good health outcomes. Consider a patient with Type 2 diabetes. Under fee-for-service, a primary care physician earns a billing code for the office visit in which they counsel the patient about diet, exercise, and medication adherence. That counseling code reimburses at approximately $85 in a typical Medicare fee schedule. If the physician spends an additional 20 minutes with the patient walking through a personalized nutrition plan, creating a written care management protocol, and coordinating with a dietitian, they may bill a care management add-on code worth an additional $40. Total revenue for doing everything right: approximately $125. Now consider what happens if the counseling fails and the patient is admitted to the hospital with a diabetic ketoacidosis crisis. The hospital admission generates approximately $8,400 in Medicare reimbursement. The specialist consultations during the admission add another $1,200. The physician who sees the patient in the hospital earns a hospital visit code. The laboratory earns from daily blood panels. The pharmacy earns from IV insulin. A preventable crisis generates approximately 80 times more revenue than the preventive care that could have avoided it. Fee-for-service does not reward the prevention of that crisis. In a narrow accounting sense, it rewards its occurrence.

Key Learning Point: Fee-for-service does not reward bad doctors or incentivize harm. Most physicians are deeply committed to their patients’ wellbeing. The problem is structural: the payment system creates financial pressure toward volume and intensity of treatment, even when lower-intensity preventive care would produce better outcomes. Individual clinicians work against this incentive every day — but the aggregate effect of the incentive on system-wide spending and outcomes is measurable and large.
What Value-Based Care Actually Means

Value-based care (VBC) is a payment philosophy, not a single program or contract type. Its core principle is simple: pay for outcomes, not for activity. Instead of paying a provider for each individual service delivered, value-based payment models reward providers for achieving defined health outcomes for a defined patient population, at a defined cost target. The shift sounds straightforward but has profound implications for how healthcare is organized, staffed, managed, and measured. Under value-based care, a primary care physician managing 500 diabetic patients is financially rewarded if the average HbA1c level across that population improves, if hospital admission rates decline, and if preventive screenings are completed. The physician earns more by keeping patients healthier — which is, intuitively, exactly what we want the payment system to incentivize.

The term “value” in healthcare has a specific technical definition, first formalized by Harvard Business School professor Michael Porter in his landmark 2006 work on healthcare strategy. Porter defined healthcare value as health outcomes achieved per dollar spent — a deceptively simple ratio with enormous implications. Improving value means either achieving better outcomes at the same cost, achieving the same outcomes at lower cost, or — ideally — achieving better outcomes at lower cost simultaneously. This framing is important because it explicitly rejects the false choice between quality and cost that has dominated American healthcare policy debates for decades. Value-based care does not argue that we should spend less on healthcare. It argues that the spending we do should produce better results, and that a payment system aligned with outcomes will, over time, naturally drive spending toward the interventions that work and away from the interventions that do not.
The Spectrum of Value-Based Models: Not All VBC Is the Same

Value-based care is not a single contract type — it is a spectrum of payment models that differ in how much financial risk is transferred from payers to providers, and how performance is measured and rewarded. Understanding this spectrum is essential because different organizations are at different stages of VBC adoption, and the policy and technology infrastructure required for advanced models is substantially more complex than what beginner models demand. At one end of the spectrum are pay-for-performance models, sometimes called P4P, in which providers continue to receive fee-for-service reimbursement but earn bonus payments — or face modest penalties — based on quality metrics. These models are low-risk for providers and easy to administer but produce only marginal incentive changes because the base fee-for-service revenue structure is unchanged. At the advanced end of the spectrum are full capitation models, in which a provider or provider organization accepts a fixed per-member per-month payment to cover all of a patient population’s healthcare needs, bearing full financial risk for both the cost and quality of care delivered.

children.text: The progression from left to right on this spectrum represents increasing provider accountability for both cost and quality, and increasing organizational complexity in terms of the data infrastructure, care management capabilities, and financial reserves required to succeed. This is why value-based care adoption has been faster among large integrated health systems with existing care management infrastructure — organizations like Kaiser Permanente, Geisinger Health System, and Intermountain Healthcare — and slower among independent rural hospitals and small physician practices that lack the population health analytics, actuarial expertise, and working capital to absorb downside financial risk. The policy challenge of accelerating VBC adoption, which we examine in depth in Module 2, is fundamentally about building the infrastructure that allows smaller and more vulnerable providers to participate in advanced models without taking on financial risk that their balance sheets cannot support.
Seeing VBC Through the Five Pillars: Why This Is Not Just an Economics Problem

One of the central insights of HTR’s analytical framework is that healthcare transformation problems cannot be solved by pulling a single lever. Value-based care is often discussed primarily as a payment reform — an economics issue. But whether VBC actually works in practice, for which patients, in which communities, and under which circumstances, is determined equally by policy design, technology infrastructure, clinical evidence, and equity architecture. This section introduces all five HTR pillars as lenses through which to examine value-based care, establishing the foundation for the four specialized modules that follow in this course.
The
Policy Pillar

asks: Is value-based care permissible, and does the regulatory environment enable or obstruct it? The answer matters enormously because VBC models require providers to share patient data across organizations, accept financial risk structures that may not have existed when their state insurance laws were written, and operate under Medicare and Medicaid payment rules that still largely default to fee-for-service. The Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 (MACRA), the Affordable Care Act’s Innovation Center (CMMI), and state-level Medicaid waiver programs are the primary policy vehicles driving VBC adoption, and understanding them is essential for any leader operating in a VBC environment.
The
Economics Pillar

asks: Is value-based care financially sustainable for providers, payers, and health systems? The economics of VBC are complex and often counterintuitive. A provider that successfully keeps patients healthy reduces its own revenue under fee-for-service — a phenomenon called the “volume-to-value transition problem.” Managing this transition requires actuarial expertise, working capital reserves, and sophisticated cost accounting capabilities that many rural and safety-net providers do not currently possess. Understanding the financial mechanics of VBC — how shared savings are calculated, what capitation rates cover, and how quality bonuses are structured — is the subject of Module 3.
The
Technology Pillar

asks: Is value-based care operationally possible without advanced data infrastructure? The honest answer is no. VBC requires providers to measure outcomes across entire patient populations, identify high-risk patients before they deteriorate, coordinate care across multiple settings, and report quality metrics to payers and CMS with precision and timeliness that fee-for-service never demanded. None of this is possible without interoperable electronic health records, health information exchange, and increasingly, artificial intelligence-powered risk stratification tools. The 34% of rural Critical Access Hospitals that lack a fully certified EHR system, and the 41% that are not connected to their state’s health information exchange, face a technology readiness barrier to advanced VBC participation that is as significant as the financial barrier. Module 4 examines this in full.
The
Clinical Pillar

asks: Does value-based care actually produce better clinical outcomes? The evidence base is growing but nuanced. Studies of CMS’s Medicare Shared Savings Program have found that mature Accountable Care Organizations — those in their fifth year or beyond — generate statistically significant reductions in hospital admissions, emergency department visits, and 30-day readmission rates compared to fee-for-service benchmarks. However, early-stage ACOs show modest or mixed results, and bundled payment programs show strong outcome improvements for high-volume procedures like hip and knee replacement but limited evidence for complex chronic disease management. The clinical evidence suggests that VBC works best when the care model underlying the payment model is also redesigned — that a new payment contract layered onto an unchanged clinical workflow produces limited results.
The
Equity Pillar

asks: Does value-based care improve health outcomes equitably, or does it reproduce and amplify existing disparities? This is the most contested question in VBC policy today, and the evidence is genuinely troubling in some dimensions. Several studies have found that providers serving high-proportions of Medicaid, low-income, and rural patients perform worse on standard VBC quality metrics not because they deliver worse care, but because their patient populations face social determinants of health — food insecurity, housing instability, transportation barriers — that are outside clinical control. If a VBC contract penalizes a rural provider for worse population health outcomes without accounting for SDOH factors, it is punishing the provider for its zip code, not its clinical performance. Module 5 examines how SDOH risk adjustment, algorithmic bias in risk stratification tools, and community health worker integration are being used to build equity into VBC architecture.
Why VBC Is the Most Credible Path Forward: The International Evidence

The case for value-based care is not purely theoretical — it is built on decades of comparative international evidence and on the documented results of early U.S. VBC programs. The countries that consistently rank highest in healthcare quality while spending significantly less than the United States share structural features that are, functionally, expressions of value-based care principles at the system level: global budgets that create accountability for population health outcomes, primary care systems that are rewarded for prevention and care coordination rather than volume, and payment mechanisms that explicitly tie reimbursement to patient outcomes rather than service counts. Germany’s Disease Management Programs, which provide structured, outcomes-linked care for chronic conditions including diabetes and coronary heart disease, have been associated with 20–28% reductions in hospital admissions for enrolled patients compared to standard care. The United Kingdom’s Quality and Outcomes Framework, a national pay-for-performance program for general practitioners, demonstrated measurable improvements in cardiovascular disease management and diabetic control rates in its first decade of operation, though subsequent research found diminishing returns as the metrics became targets to be managed rather than genuine outcome measures.

Within the United States, the most mature evidence base for VBC effectiveness comes from the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), which CMS launched in 2012 under the Affordable Care Act. By 2025, MSSP included 480 Accountable Care Organizations covering 11.2 million Medicare beneficiaries. The program’s cumulative results through 2024 show net Medicare savings of $18.7 billion relative to fee-for-service benchmark spending, with quality scores across participating ACOs consistently outperforming non-ACO fee-for-service providers on 24 of 28 standard quality metrics. Critically, ACOs in their fifth year or beyond — mature organizations that have had time to build care management infrastructure and redesign clinical workflows — generate 2.3 times the per-beneficiary savings of ACOs in their first two years, suggesting that the VBC model rewards organizational investment in transformation over time in ways that fee-for-service structurally cannot.

children.text: The international data in the table above reveals a pattern that is difficult to argue with: the countries with the lowest avoidable mortality rates and the highest life expectancy are, without exception, countries that direct a higher proportion of healthcare spending toward primary care and operate under payment systems that link reimbursement to outcomes rather than volume. The United States directs only 6% of healthcare spending toward primary care — the lowest proportion of any wealthy nation — while directing the largest share toward high-cost specialty and hospital care. This is not an accident. It is the predictable result of a fee-for-service payment system that reimburses a 15-minute primary care visit at $85 and a 45-minute cardiac catheterization at $3,200. When you pay for procedures, you get procedures. When you pay for health, you get health.

Every additional dollar the United States spends on hospital and specialist care relative to peer nations is, in the aggregate, a dollar that does not flow to the preventive and primary care infrastructure that would reduce the need for that hospital and specialist care in the first place. We are paying for the consequence and underpaying for the prevention. That is the fee-for-service trap. — Dr. Don Berwick, former CMS Administrator and Institute for Healthcare Improvement founder, JAMA Health Forum, 2024.
The Honest Challenges: Why VBC Is Harder Than It Sounds

Value-based care is not a magic switch. Understanding its genuine implementation challenges is as important as understanding its theoretical promise, and any course that presents VBC as a straightforward solution to a complex problem is doing learners a disservice. The transition from fee-for-service to value-based payment creates real financial risk for providers during the transition period. A hospital system that begins reducing unnecessary hospitalizations and emergency visits through better care management is simultaneously reducing its own revenue under the portion of its contracts that remain fee-for-service. For a health system operating at a 1–3% operating margin — which describes the majority of rural and community hospitals in the United States — a 5% reduction in inpatient volume while VBC contracts ramp up can create a cash flow crisis that threatens financial stability before the VBC savings materialize. This is the volume-to-value transition problem, and it is the primary reason that smaller providers have been slower to adopt advanced VBC models.

A second genuine challenge is the measurement problem. Value-based care requires measuring outcomes — but measuring outcomes in healthcare is genuinely hard. Unlike a manufacturing process where defect rates can be counted precisely, health outcomes are influenced by dozens of variables outside clinical control, including patients’ genetics, behaviors, economic circumstances, housing stability, and social support networks. A diabetic patient who has adequate food, a safe neighborhood for walking, and a job with health insurance is far more likely to achieve target HbA1c levels than an identically diagnosed patient who is food insecure, living in a neighborhood without sidewalks, and uninsured. If a VBC contract measures both providers on the same HbA1c outcome metric without adjusting for these social differences, it is not measuring quality of care — it is measuring the zip code of the patient population. Getting outcome measurement right — risk-adjusting for social determinants, selecting metrics that reflect clinical decisions rather than patient circumstances — is the equity challenge at the heart of VBC that Module 5 examines in depth.

For Learners and Practitioners: If you work in or with a healthcare organization currently in a VBC contract, ask three questions: (1) How are our quality metrics risk-adjusted for social determinants of health? (2) What percentage of our total revenue is now value-based versus fee-for-service, and what is the organization’s three-year target? (3) Do we have the data infrastructure to track our attributed patient population’s outcomes in real time? The answers will tell you more about your organization’s VBC readiness than any strategic plan document.
Key Federal Programs Moving the U.S. Toward Value: What You Need to Know

The federal government has been the primary driver of VBC adoption in the United States, primarily through CMS’s Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), which was established by the Affordable Care Act in 2010 with a 10-year mandatory funding appropriation of $10 billion specifically to design, test, and scale alternative payment models. CMMI has launched more than 50 payment model pilots since 2011, covering everything from bundled payments for surgical episodes to fully capitated primary care models. Not all have succeeded — CMMI has also terminated models that did not demonstrate savings or quality improvements — but the cumulative evidence base it has generated is the most comprehensive real-world VBC dataset that exists anywhere in the world, and the models that have survived and scaled represent the practical playbook for VBC implementation in the U.S. context.
The
Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP)

is the largest VBC program in the world by covered lives, with 480 ACOs and 11.2 million beneficiaries as of 2025. It allows physician groups and health systems to form Accountable Care Organizations that share in the savings they generate relative to a fee-for-service spending benchmark, with quality performance gates that must be cleared before savings are distributed. MSSP is the entry point for most organizations beginning their VBC journey and the primary subject of Module 3’s economics analysis.
The
CMS AHEAD Model (All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development)

is CMS’s most ambitious current VBC initiative, launched in 2023 and currently operating in eight states. AHEAD moves beyond Medicare to create all-payer global budgets — meaning that all payers in a participating state, including Medicaid, commercial insurers, and Medicare, operate under a coordinated spending target. It is the closest the United States has come to a national health budget model, and its early results in Maryland — which has operated under a hospital global budget since 1977 — are the most compelling domestic evidence that global budget models can simultaneously improve quality, reduce spending growth, and advance equity.
The
BPCI Advanced Program (Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced)

bundles all Medicare payments for a defined clinical episode — a hip replacement, a pneumonia hospitalization, a cardiac bypass surgery — into a single target price. If the provider delivers the episode of care for less than the target price while meeting quality thresholds, they keep the difference. If they spend more, they repay the excess. BPCI Advanced covers 32 clinical episodes and has demonstrated the strongest cost and quality evidence of any CMS bundled payment model, particularly for high-volume surgical procedures.
The
Primary Care First Model

is CMMI’s effort to bring advanced primary care practices into a capitation-adjacent payment structure without the full actuarial complexity of a Medicare Advantage-style model. Participating practices receive a flat per-patient per-month payment plus a performance-based adjustment tied to reducing acute hospitalizations. It is specifically designed for independent primary care practices that want to move toward VBC without the organizational infrastructure of a large ACO, making it the most relevant federal program for rural and small-practice environments.

children.text: Module 1 Summary: What You Should Now Understand

We have covered substantial ground in this first module, and it is worth consolidating the core ideas before moving to the more specialized analysis in Modules 2 through 5. The United States healthcare crisis is, at its root, a payment architecture problem: a fee-for-service system that was designed for a world of acute episodic illness is being applied to a world of chronic disease and complex care needs, producing the highest spending and among the worst outcomes of any wealthy nation. Value-based care is not a single program or a policy slogan — it is a logical structural response to that misalignment, grounded in the principle that what you pay for determines what you get. The international evidence and the growing domestic evidence base from MSSP, BPCI Advanced, and the AHEAD Model all point in the same direction: systems that pay for outcomes, strengthen primary care, and hold providers accountable for population health — rather than for the volume of services delivered — produce better results at lower cost.

At the same time, value-based care is not a solved problem. The volume-to-value transition creates real financial risk for providers, particularly smaller and rural organizations with thin operating margins. Outcome measurement remains technically and politically contested, especially when social determinants of health create outcome differences that are not within clinical control. And the technology, policy, and equity infrastructure required for advanced VBC models to work fairly and effectively is still being built. The remaining four modules of this course examine each of these dimensions in depth — not to discourage you about VBC’s prospects, but to equip you with the complete picture that any leader operating in this environment needs to navigate it successfully.
Your Personal VBC Readiness Self-Assessment

Before moving to Module 2, use these five questions to benchmark your current understanding and identify the areas where this course will add the most value for your specific role and organization. There are no right or wrong answers — honest self-assessment is the foundation of effective learning, and research on professional education consistently shows that learners who enter a new module with an explicit awareness of their own knowledge gaps retain substantially more than those who proceed without reflection.

Can you explain to a colleague, in plain language and without jargon, the specific mechanism by which fee-for-service creates a financial incentive against preventive care? If not, re-read the section on the incentive problem before proceeding.

Do you know which of the six VBC model types on the spectrum your organization currently operates under for its Medicare and Medicaid contracts? If not, this is a conversation to have with your CFO or contract management team before Module 3.

Can you name the three federal programs — MSSP, AHEAD, and BPCI Advanced — and describe in one sentence what each one does? If not, re-read the ‘Key Federal Programs’ section above before proceeding to Module 2’s policy deep-dive.

Do you understand why the Equity Pillar identifies outcome measurement as a potential source of disparity amplification in VBC contracts? If the SDOH risk-adjustment issue was new to you, make a note to pay particular attention to Module 5.

What is the single most important question about value-based care that this module did not answer for you? Write it down. The remaining four modules are designed to answer the most common versions of that question — and if yours is not covered, use the HTR Academy discussion forum to raise it with the course faculty.
Fee-for-service pays for activity. Value-based care pays for outcomes. This is the foundational distinction, and everything else in this course builds on it.

The U.S. spends $13,493 per capita on healthcare — nearly twice the OECD average — and ranks 46th in life expectancy. The primary structural cause is a payment system that does not reward health, only treatment.

VBC exists on a spectrum from low-risk pay-for-performance models to full capitation. Different organizations are at different stages, and the infrastructure required scales with the model’s complexity and risk level.

All five HTR pillars — Policy, Economics, Technology, Clinical, and Equity — are required to fully evaluate whether VBC works, for whom, and under what conditions. Examining VBC through only one lens produces an incomplete and potentially misleading picture.

Three federal programs are the primary vehicles of U.S. VBC adoption today: the Medicare Shared Savings Program (11.2M beneficiaries), the AHEAD Model (8 states, all-payer global budgets), and BPCI Advanced (32 clinical episode bundles). Understanding these programs is essential for any healthcare leader operating in a Medicare or Medicaid environment.

body.title: HTR Academy Podcast: Value-Based Care Fundamentals — A Conversation with the Course Authors
body.summary: In this 55-minute companion audio to Module 1, HTR Chief Intelligence Officer Dr. Sarah Chen and Principal Economist Marcus Webb discuss the historical arc of fee-for-service in American medicine, walk through the international comparison data in detail, and answer the most common questions from healthcare professionals encountering value-based care concepts for the first time. The conversation includes a frank assessment of why VBC adoption has been slower than its proponents projected a decade ago, and what the evidence from mature ACOs tells us about the conditions under which the model genuinely delivers on its promise.

body.caption: This 18-minute animated explainer video, produced by HTR Academy’s visual learning team, walks through the fee-for-service incentive problem using the plumber analogy from this module, then builds the value-based care spectrum diagram step by step, illustrating how each model type shifts financial risk and quality accountability between payers and providers. The video is designed for use in team training sessions and board education presentations and is available with closed captioning and a downloadable slide deck for HTR Academy subscribers.
